title: Alive, once alive, never alive: the signs of life

summary.text: A crow, a mint leaf and a steel spoon sit on the same windowsill. Only the crow and the mint are alive. Living things eat, grow, move, breathe and have young. Some things were alive once, like a wooden spoon or a dry leaf. Some things were never alive, like a stone or a steel spoon. In this unit you sort the things in your kitchen, and find out if a picked mint leaf is still alive.
summary.art: A windowsill with a crow on the edge, a glass of fresh mint, a wooden spoon and a steel spoon in a row, and a small child looking at them with chin in hands.

intro.hook: Hold a fresh mint leaf in one hand and a steel spoon in the other. Both are cool. Both stay still. Which one is alive?
intro.text: Most children say the mint leaf. But how can we tell? The spoon does not move, and the leaf does not move either. Scientists look for signs of life. A living thing eats, grows, moves, breathes and has young. A spoon does none of these. In this unit we test some of these signs at home, on mint leaves, on our breath and on ourselves.
intro.art: A child's two open hands, one holding a green mint leaf and the other a shiny steel spoon, with a big question mark between them.

outcomes: By the end I can say if a thing is alive, was once alive, or was never alive, and give one reason.
By the end I can name the signs of life: eating, growing, moving, breathing and having young.
By the end I can say that plants are alive too, and show one sign of life in a plant.
By the end I can match a mother animal to her young.
By the end I can make a guess, look carefully, and say if my guess was right.

terms.meaning: Alive means living. A living thing eats, grows, moves, breathes and has young.
terms.example: You are alive. So is a crow, an ant and the tulsi plant on the balcony.
terms.art: A crow, an ant and a tulsi plant in a pot, side by side.

terms.meaning: A thing that was never alive has never eaten, grown or breathed. It is not made from a living thing.
terms.example: A stone, a steel spoon, salt and water were never alive.
terms.art: A grey stone, a steel spoon and a small heap of salt on a plate.

terms.meaning: A thing that was once alive was part of a living thing, but is not living now.
terms.example: A wooden spoon came from a tree. A cotton shirt came from a cotton plant. A dry tej patta was a leaf on a tree.
terms.art: A wooden spoon, a folded cotton shirt and a dry tej patta leaf in a row.

terms.meaning: To breathe is to take in air and let air out again. All living things breathe in some way.
terms.example: Breathe out on a cold steel plate. The cloudy patch shows the wet air from inside you.
terms.art: A child breathing out on a steel plate, with a cloudy patch on it.

terms.meaning: The young of a living thing are their babies. Young grow up to be like their parents.
terms.example: A chick is the young of a hen. A calf is the young of a cow. A seed grows into a young plant.
terms.art: A hen with three chicks, and a cow with her calf.

explanations.definition: A living thing eats, grows, moves, breathes and has young. It also senses the world around it.
explanations.description: One sign alone does not tell us. A car moves, but it does not grow or have baby cars. A crow does all of these things. So does a mango tree, only more slowly. Animals eat food. Plants make their own food in their green leaves, using sunlight, air and water. Living things also feel what is around them. A cat hears her name. A plant feels the light.
examples: A crow eats, flies, breathes and lays eggs.
A baby grows, drinks milk and breathes, and will one day be able to have babies.
A toy car moves, but it never eats or grows.
explanations.context: This card says how we can tell if something is alive.
explanations.art: Five small pictures in a row: a crow eating, a child growing taller, a dog running, a child breathing out, a hen with chicks.

explanations.definition: Once alive means the thing was part of a living thing, but is not living now. Never alive means it was never part of a living thing.
explanations.description: Look around the kitchen. A wooden spoon came from a tree, so it was once alive. Paper is made from trees too. A cotton cloth came from a cotton plant. A dry tej patta was a leaf. A steel spoon, salt, water and a stone were never alive. They were never part of a living thing.
examples: A wooden chopping board was once alive.
A coconut shell was once alive.
A steel tumbler was never alive.
explanations.context: This card is about the things that are not alive now. Some of them were alive once.
explanations.art: Two baskets: one with a wooden spoon, a coconut shell and a dry leaf, the other with a steel tumbler, a stone and a spoon of salt.

explanations.definition: Plants eat, grow, move, breathe and have young, just like animals, only in their own way.
explanations.description: Plants make their own food in their green leaves. They breathe through tiny holes in their leaves, too small to see. They grow taller and make new leaves. They move slowly. A plant on a windowsill turns their leaves to the light over a few days. Plants also have young. A tomato is full of seeds, and each seed can grow into a new tomato plant.
examples: A tulsi plant grows new leaves every week.
A money plant on a window turns their leaves to face the light.
A cut tomato shows many seeds, which are the young of the tomato plant.
explanations.context: This card says why plants are alive, even though they seem to stay still.
explanations.art: A money plant in a pot on a sunny window, all their leaves turned towards the glass.

explanations.concept: Is a picked leaf still alive?
explanations.description: A leaf picked from a plant does not die at once. In our mint test, droopy picked mint stood up again in water. Picked mint can even grow new roots in a glass of water. But a picked leaf cannot make new seeds alone, and after some days it dries up. So people answer this question in different ways.
examples: Droopy picked mint stands up firm again in a cup of water.
A mint sprig in water grows white roots in about one or two weeks.
A dry tej patta in water stays dry and brown inside.

perspectives.explanation: The leaf is still alive for some days, because the tiny parts inside the leaf are still living. That is why the droopy mint could fill up with water again.
A picked leaf is a living part, not a whole living plant. The leaf cannot live on for long unless it grows roots of its own.

explanations.context: This card is about the mint test, where a droopy picked mint sprig stood up again in water.
explanations.art: Two glasses: one with a droopy mint sprig, one with the same sprig standing firm, and a clock between them showing one hour passing.

explanations.description: Plants feel light, touch, water and warmth, and they act on what they feel. Roots grow towards water. Leaves turn towards light. Some scientists say these actions are automatic, because plants have no brain.
examples: A plant on a window turns their leaves to the light.
Roots grow down and towards wet soil.
A droopy plant stands up again after a drink of water.

perspectives.who: Many people who study plants closely
perspectives.explanation: Plants feel, remember and decide. They sense light and water and choose where to grow.
Plants have no brain, so their actions are automatic, like a door that closes by itself.

explanations.context: This card is about whether plants feel what is around them.
explanations.art: A small plant on a windowsill, the leaves turned to the sunlight and the roots in a clear glass pot reaching down towards the water.

agreed.text: Living things eat, grow, move, breathe and have young.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have watched millions of kinds of living things, from tiny bacteria to elephants and trees. All of them do these things.
Plants grow, make their own food, breathe through tiny holes in their leaves and make seeds that grow into new plants.

agreed.text: Every living thing comes from another living thing.
agreed.evidence: A chick hatches from a hen's egg. A plant grows from a seed. A caterpillar hatches from a butterfly's egg. Nobody has ever seen a living thing start from mud or stone.

challenging.claim: Anything that moves by itself is alive.
challenging.who: A very common idea, among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: Most things that move by themselves are animals, like a dog, a crow or an ant.
challenging.against: A ceiling fan, a river and the wind move, and they are not alive. In 1827, Robert Brown, a Scottish plant scientist, saw tiny bits jiggling in water under a microscope. At first he wondered if they were alive. Then he saw dust from rock and glass jiggle in the same way. So moving alone does not mean alive.
challenging.context: This card is about a common mistake: that moving means alive.

challenging.claim: Plants are not really living, because they stay in one place.
challenging.who: A common idea among young children
challenging.for: A plant does not walk or run, and we rarely see a plant move.
challenging.against: Plants grow, eat, breathe and make seeds. They move too, only slowly: leaves turn to light, and roots grow down. A plant moved to a window turns their leaves towards the light in a few days.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that plants are not alive.

challenging.claim: Fire is alive, because fire eats wood, needs air and grows.
challenging.who: A puzzle many children and philosophers have raised
challenging.for: A fire grows bigger, needs air to keep going and spreads to new places.
challenging.against: A fire has no body that builds itself from food. A fire only burns the wood up and leaves ash. Scientists say fire is not alive.
challenging.context: This card is about a tricky case: fire.

big_questions.q: When we pick a leaf, when does the leaf stop being alive?
big_questions.hint: Think of the droopy mint that stood up again in water. Was it still alive?

big_questions.q: A wooden spoon was once part of a living tree. Is any of the tree still in the spoon?
big_questions.hint: Look closely at the lines in the wood. They are the lines of the tree growing, year after year.

big_questions.q: You were a tiny baby once. You grew. What did your body grow from?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you eat every day: rice, dal, milk, fruit.

big_questions.q: Can something be a little bit alive?
big_questions.hint: Think of a dry seed in a packet, or a picked leaf in water.

story.title: The Stone in the Tulsi Pot
story.note: The snail facts are true for most land snails: eyes on the tips of the long tentacles, a breathing hole on the side near the shell, a rough tongue called a radula, and small eggs laid in damp soil. Anjali, Kiran and Ajji are made up.
text: It was the first week of the monsoon in Mumbai. The rain had stopped, and the air smelled of wet earth. Anjali was six. She went out on the balcony to look at her plants.
Her little cousin Kiran came running after her. He was four, and he was staying with them for the holidays. 'Anju Akka, look!' he shouted. 'A stone in your tulsi pot!'
Anjali bent down. On the wet soil sat a round brown thing, the size of a big marble. It was hard and shiny, and it had a curl on top, like a swirl of jalebi. It did not move at all.
'Is it a stone?' Kiran asked.
Anjali did not know. She called her grandmother, who was drinking tea inside. Ajji came out slowly, with her glasses on her nose. She looked at the brown thing for a long time.
'What do you think?' Ajji asked Anjali. 'How can we find out if this is a stone?'
Anjali thought. 'A stone stays where you put it,' she said. 'Let's leave it, and look again in the morning.'
So they left the brown thing in the tulsi pot. Before bed, Anjali put a little stick next to it, to mark the spot.

In the morning, Anjali ran to the balcony. The brown thing was not next to the stick any more. It was on the edge of the pot. And from the stick to the edge, there was a thin silver line, shining on the soil.
'It moved!' said Anjali. 'Stones do not move by themselves. Something left that silver line.'
Kiran's eyes were big. Then Anjali saw something else. One tulsi leaf had a hole in it, with neat, round edges. It had not been there yesterday.
'And it ate my tulsi!' said Anjali. 'Stones do not eat.'
Ajji smiled and fetched a small steel plate. She put a wet cabbage leaf on it and set the brown thing gently beside it. 'Now, sit very still,' she said. 'Living things are often shy.'

They sat on the balcony floor and waited. For a long time, nothing happened. Kiran started to wriggle. Then, slowly, something soft and grey came out from under the brown curl. Out came a head with two long horns, and on the tip of each horn was a tiny black dot.
'A snail!' whispered Anjali. 'The round thing is a shell. The snail lives inside.'
'Those dots are the snail's eyes,' said Ajji. 'They are at the top of the long horns. And look there, near the shell, on the snail's side.'
Anjali looked. A little hole opened, then closed, then opened again.
'That is how a snail breathes,' said Ajji. 'Air goes in and out of that hole.'
The snail moved onto the cabbage and began to eat. They could hear a tiny scratching sound. 'Snails have a rough tongue, like a file,' said Ajji. 'They scrape the leaf with it.'
Kiran clapped his hands. 'Snail, you eat, you move and you breathe,' he said. 'You are alive!'
Later that day, Anjali found another round shell behind the pot. This one was white and dry, and very light. She looked inside. It was empty.
'Is this one alive?' Kiran asked.
Anjali turned the shell over in her hand. 'No,' she said. 'This shell was once part of a living snail. But no snail lives in it now. It is once alive, like a dry leaf.'
'And a stone?' asked Kiran.
'A stone was never alive,' said Anjali. 'A stone never ate, and never moved, and never had babies.'
Ajji nodded. 'Snails lay tiny eggs in wet soil,' she said. 'If you are lucky, there will be baby snails in the pots next month, no bigger than a grain of rice.'
That evening, Anjali put the snail back in the tulsi pot, with the cabbage leaf. 'You can stay,' she told the snail. 'But please eat the cabbage and leave my tulsi.'
The snail did not say anything. But the next morning, the cabbage was full of holes, and the tulsi was not.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Anjali tests the brown thing for signs of life, one by one. It moves, eats and breathes, so it is alive. The empty shell was once alive. A stone was never alive.
ask: How did Anjali find out that the brown thing was not a stone?
Why was the empty white shell 'once alive', and not 'never alive'?
What other living thing might live on your balcony or window?
art: A girl and a small boy bending over a tulsi pot on a wet city balcony, looking at a round brown snail shell on the soil.
A thin silver trail on the soil from a small stick to the edge of the pot.
A grandmother, a girl and a boy sitting on a balcony floor, watching a snail with long horns come out to eat a cabbage leaf on a steel plate.
A girl holding an empty white snail shell up to the light.

games.title: Mother and Baby: a matching game
games.context: This is a memory game about having young. Every living thing has young, and the young grow up to be like their parents. Players find the parent and the young that belong together.

printables.title: 20 cards to cut out: 10 parents and their 10 young

items.b: Parent. Her young is a chick.
Young. Grows up to be a hen or a rooster.
Parent. Her young is a calf.
Young. Grows up to be a cow or a bull.
Parent. Her young is a tadpole.
Young. Grows legs and becomes a frog.
Parent. Her young is a caterpillar.
Young. Becomes a butterfly.
Parent. Her young is a calf.
Young. Drinks milk for about two years.
Parent. Her young is a puppy.
Young. Grows up to be a dog.
Parent. Her young is a chick that hatches from an egg.
Young. Grows feathers and learns to fly.
Parent. Her young is a baby.
Young. Grows up to be a grown-up.
Parent. Their young grow from mango seeds.
Young. Grows up to be a mango tree.
Parent. Their young grow from the seeds inside a tomato.
Young. Grows up to be a tomato plant.

rules: Before you play, draw the living thing on each card under the name, so a child who cannot read can play.
Mix the cards and lay them face down in rows.
On your turn, turn over two cards and say what they are.
If they are a parent and their young, keep the pair and have another turn.
If not, turn them back over in the same places. The next player has a turn.
When all the cards are matched, the player with the most pairs wins.

flow.do: 1. Read each card name to your child. 2. Help your child draw a small picture on each card. 3. Mix the cards and lay them face down in four rows of five.
flow.say: Every living thing has young. Let's make our cards first. You draw the hen, I'll read the next name.
flow.kid: Draw a picture on each card. A hen. A chick. A cow. Then mix them up.

flow.do: 1. Take turns turning over two cards. 2. Read the names aloud for your child. 3. When a pair is found, ask the question below.
flow.say: Turn over two cards. Is that a mother and her baby? How do you know?
flow.kid: Turn over two cards. Do they go together? Keep them if they do.

ask.q: The tadpole looks nothing like a frog. How do we know a tadpole is a young frog?
good: Because a tadpole grows legs and turns into a frog.
Because a frog lays eggs and tadpoles hatch from them.

flow.do: Count the pairs. Then pick up the mango tree pair and ask the check question.
flow.say: Who has the most pairs? Now, a plant question.
flow.kid: Count your pairs. Who has the most?

check.q: Does a mango tree have young?
options: Yes, a mango seed grows into a young mango tree
check.why: Plants have young too. Each mango seed can grow into a new mango tree. Having young is a sign of life for plants and animals.

setup.art: Twenty small cards on a table, each with a name and a child's drawing: hen, chick, cow, calf, frog, tadpole and more.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a living thing on each card.

setup.art: Cards laid face down in four rows of five, with two cards turned up: a hen and a chick.
setup.caption: 2. Turn over two cards. Find a parent and their young.

games.title: Wiggle, Sit or Statue
games.players: 1 or more players and a caller
games.context: This is a moving game about alive, once alive and never alive. The caller says a thing, and the players move to show which kind of thing it is.

items.b: Alive: wiggle
Alive: wiggle
Alive: wiggle
Alive: wiggle
Alive: wiggle
Alive: wiggle
Once alive: sit down
Once alive: sit down
Once alive: sit down
Once alive: sit down
Once alive: sit down
Once alive: sit down
Never alive: freeze like a statue
Never alive: freeze like a statue
Never alive: freeze like a statue
Never alive: freeze like a statue
Never alive: freeze like a statue
Never alive: freeze like a statue

rules: The caller mixes the cards and reads one out loud.
If the thing is alive, the players wiggle like a living thing.
If the thing was once alive, the players sit down on the floor.
If the thing was never alive, the players freeze like a statue.
The caller turns the card over and reads the answer. Talk about any surprises.
After every six cards, a player becomes the caller.

flow.do: 1. Clear a space on the floor. 2. Show the three moves: wiggle, sit down, freeze.
flow.say: Let's learn the moves. Alive, wiggle. Once alive, sit down. Never alive, freeze like a statue.
flow.kid: Alive? Wiggle! Once alive? Sit down! Never alive? Freeze!

flow.do: 1. Read one card at a time. 2. Wait for your child to move. 3. Read the back of the card.
flow.say: Ready? A wooden spoon! Now tell me, why did you sit down?
flow.kid: Listen to the word. Wiggle, sit or freeze?

good: Because paper is made from trees.
Because it came from a tree that was alive.

flow.parent: Paper is made mostly from wood, so a newspaper was once alive. A ceiling fan moves, but it is never alive. Let your child argue, then read the card.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: One tricky one. The fan moves round and round. Why did we freeze for the fan?
flow.kid: The fan moves. Is the fan alive?

check.q: The ceiling fan moves. Is the fan alive?
options: No, the fan does not eat, grow or have young
Only when the fan is switched on
check.why: Moving is not enough. A living thing also eats, grows, breathes and has young. A fan does none of these, so a fan was never alive.

setup.art: A child wiggling on a living room floor while a grandmother reads a card that says 'A crow'.
setup.caption: 1. Alive? Wiggle like a living thing.

setup.art: The same child sitting on the floor, then standing frozen like a statue, with cards for 'A wooden spoon' and 'A stone'.
setup.caption: 2. Once alive? Sit down. Never alive? Freeze.

experiments.title: Droopy Mint: is a picked leaf still alive?
experiments.context: In this experiment you put droopy picked mint, a dry tej patta and a paper leaf into water. Then you wait one hour and see which ones change. This tells us if picked mint is still alive.
experiments.question: Is mint that was picked from the plant still alive? What happens to droopy mint, a dry leaf and a paper leaf in water?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which ones will stand up in water: the droopy mint, the dry tej patta, or the paper leaf? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Each thing gets the same cup and the same water, for the same time. One droopy mint sprig stays on a dry plate, so we can see what water does.

materials.item: fresh mint (pudina) sprigs from the market, left out on a plate for 2 or 3 hours until they droop
a dry tej patta (bay leaf) from the kitchen
a leaf shape cut from newspaper, with a long paper stalk
steel tumblers or glasses of water

schedule.what: Feel the three leaves. Guess. Put them in water. Wait one hour. Feel them again and draw what you see.

experiments.record: Draw the three cups and the plate, before and after. Circle the ones that changed.

flow.do: 1. Two or three hours before, leave two mint sprigs on a plate in the room until they go floppy. 2. Now lay out the two droopy sprigs, the tej patta and the paper leaf. 3. Let your child touch each one.
flow.say: Touch each leaf gently. How does each one feel?
flow.kid: Touch each leaf. Is it soft? Is it crisp? Is it floppy?

ask.q: Which of these was once part of a plant?
good: The mint and the tej patta.
The mint and the tej patta came from plants. The paper is made from trees too.

flow.parent: The mint should be floppy but still green, not dry and crisp. Coriander or palak leaves work too if you have no mint. Paper is made from wood, so it was once alive too. That is fine: it is now a flat sheet, not a leaf.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess, and to say why. Write the guess down.
flow.say: We will put each one in water. Which ones will stand up again? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Which will stand up in water? Why?

good: The mint will stand up, because it is still a bit alive.
The paper will go soggy, because paper soaks up water.

flow.do: 1. Snip a little off the bottom of one mint stalk. 2. Stand that sprig in a tumbler of water. 3. Stand the tej patta in the second tumbler and the paper leaf in the third. 4. Leave the second mint sprig on the dry plate.
flow.say: Each one gets its own cup of water. This mint sprig stays on the dry plate, so we can see what the water does.
flow.kid: Put each leaf in a cup of water. One mint stays on the plate.
flow.parent: Cutting the end opens the stalk so water can go in. Put the cups in the shade, not in hot sun.

flow.do: Leave the cups for one hour. Play Wiggle, Sit or Statue, or do the steel plate breath test, while you wait.
flow.say: Now we wait one hour. Living things need time.
flow.kid: Now we wait one hour.
flow.wait: Leave the cups for one hour.

flow.do: 1. Look at each cup together. 2. Let your child touch each leaf again. 3. Compare the mint in water with the mint on the plate.
flow.say: Look and touch. What happened to each one?
flow.kid: Look at each cup. Touch each leaf. What changed?

ask.q: What happened to the mint in water?
good: The mint stood up straight.
The mint feels firm and fresh again.

ask.q: What happened to the tej patta and the paper?
good: The tej patta stayed dry and brown.
The paper went soggy and flopped over.

flow.parent: The mint in water usually stands up firm within an hour. If it is still droopy, wait one more hour. The mint on the plate stays droopy or gets worse. The tej patta stays brown and stiff. The paper goes soft and floppy.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw, and why. Then draw the cups together.
flow.say: So, is the picked mint still alive? What did you see that tells you?
flow.kid: Is the mint still alive? Say what you saw. Then draw it.

ask.q: Why did only the mint stand up?
good: Because the mint is still alive, so it can drink the water.
Because the tej patta is dry and dead, and paper was never a leaf like that.

flow.parent: A strong answer uses what your child saw: the mint stood up in water, and the dry leaf did not. The living parts inside the mint fill up with water and push the leaf firm. Dry, dead leaves cannot do this.

check.q: The droopy mint stood up in water, but the dry tej patta did not. What does this tell us?
options: Water makes every leaf stand up
The picked mint was still alive
The tej patta was never a leaf
check.why: Water did not make the tej patta or the paper stand up. Only the mint stood up, because the mint was still alive. Living leaves fill up with water and go firm.

setup.art: A plate with two droopy mint sprigs, one dry brown tej patta and one leaf shape cut from newspaper.
setup.caption: 1. Feel the droopy mint, the dry tej patta and the paper leaf.

setup.art: Three steel tumblers of water in a row: one with a mint sprig, one with a tej patta, one with a paper leaf, and a mint sprig lying on a dry plate beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Put each one in water. Leave one mint sprig on a dry plate.

setup.art: The same tumblers an hour later: the mint standing up green and firm, the tej patta unchanged, the paper leaf soggy and bent over.
setup.caption: 3. After one hour, look and touch again.

activities.title: Three Plates: sort the kitchen
activities.context: In this activity you collect things from the kitchen and sort them onto three plates: alive, once alive and never alive.

materials.item: three plates, labelled with a drawing: a smiling plant (alive), a leaf with a tick (once alive), a stone (never alive)

about 10 things from the kitchen: a potato, a wooden spoon, a steel spoon, salt, a coconut shell or piece, a cotton cloth, a dry tej patta, a glass marble or stone, a sprig of mint in water, a paper bag

schedule.what: Collect 10 kitchen things. Sort them onto three plates. Say why for each one.

activities.record: Draw your three plates and what went on each one.

flow.do: 1. Put out the three plates. 2. Show your child the drawing on each plate. 3. Bring out the kitchen things one at a time.
flow.say: This plate is for things that are alive now. This one is for things that were once alive. This one is for things that were never alive.
flow.kid: Look at the three plates. Alive. Once alive. Never alive.

flow.do: 1. Hand your child one thing at a time. 2. Let them put it on a plate. 3. Ask why.
flow.say: Where does the wooden spoon go? Why?
flow.kid: Pick up one thing. Which plate? Why?

ask.q: Why does the wooden spoon go on the 'once alive' plate?
good: Because the wooden spoon was made from a tree.
Because wood comes from a tree, and the tree was alive.

flow.parent: Don't correct at first. Ask 'why?' and let the reasons come. A potato is alive: leave one in a cupboard for a few weeks and shoots grow. Salt, steel and a marble were never alive. Cotton came from a cotton plant, so it was once alive.

flow.do: Pick up the potato and ask the question below.
flow.say: Here is a tricky one. Is the potato alive?
flow.kid: Is the potato alive? What do you think?

good: Yes, because a potato can grow shoots and become a new plant.

flow.parent: A potato in a dark cupboard grows pale shoots after a few weeks. So a potato is alive, resting and waiting to grow.

setup.art: Three steel plates on a kitchen floor, each with a small drawing on a paper label: a plant, a leaf, a stone.
setup.caption: 1. Put out three plates: alive, once alive, never alive.

setup.art: A child placing a wooden spoon on the middle plate, with a steel spoon and salt on the third plate and a potato and mint on the first.
setup.caption: 2. Put each thing on a plate. Say why.

activities.title: Breath on a Steel Plate
activities.context: In this activity you breathe out on a cool steel plate and see a cloudy patch. Then you test a doll or a toy. Breathing is a sign of life.

materials.item: a cool steel plate or a mirror
a doll or a soft toy

schedule.what: Breathe out on a steel plate. Hold the plate near a toy's mouth. Compare.

activities.record: Draw the plate with your breath patch, and the plate near the toy.

flow.do: 1. Hold the plate a hand's width from your child's mouth. 2. Ask them to breathe out slowly, with an open mouth, like a 'haaa'.
flow.say: Breathe out on the plate, slowly. Haaa. What do you see?
flow.kid: Hold the plate near your mouth. Say haaa. Look!

ask.q: What do you see on the plate?
good: A cloudy patch.
The plate went foggy, then it went away.

flow.parent: The breath we breathe out is warm and wet. On a cool plate the wetness makes a cloudy patch, which soon disappears. A plate from the fridge shelf, or a mirror, works best.

flow.do: 1. Hold the plate in front of the doll's mouth for a while. 2. Then in front of your own mouth.
flow.say: Now let's try the doll. Does the doll breathe on the plate?
flow.kid: Hold the plate near the doll. Is there a cloudy patch?

check.q: The plate went cloudy near your mouth, but not near the doll. Why?
options: You breathe, and the doll does not
check.why: You breathe in air and breathe out warm, wet air. The doll was never alive and does not breathe. Breathing is one sign of life.

setup.art: A child breathing 'haaa' onto a steel plate held by a grown-up, with a cloudy patch on the plate.
setup.caption: 1. Breathe out on a cool steel plate.

setup.art: The same plate held in front of a doll's face, with no cloudy patch.
setup.caption: 2. Try the doll. Compare.

activities.title: I Am Growing: my hand now and later
activities.context: In this activity you draw round your hand and keep the drawing. You also try on something you wore as a baby. Growing is a sign of life.

materials.item: a sheet of paper and a pencil
a baby vest, sock or cap your child wore, or a baby photo

schedule.what: Draw round your hand. Write the date. Try on a baby sock or cap. Keep the drawing in a safe place.

activities.record: Keep the hand drawing with the date. Draw round your hand again in six months, on top of the old one.

flow.do: 1. Put your child's hand flat on the paper. 2. Draw round it. 3. Write the date beside it.
flow.say: Let's draw round your hand. We'll keep it and see if your hand grows.
flow.kid: Put your hand flat on the paper. Keep still. Now look!

flow.do: Bring out the baby vest, sock or photo. Let your child try it on or hold it next to themselves.
flow.say: You wore this when you were a baby. Does it fit now? Why not?
flow.kid: Try on your baby sock. Does it fit?

ask.q: Why doesn't the baby sock fit any more?
good: Because I grew bigger.
Because my feet grew.

flow.do: Ask where the new body comes from.
flow.say: You grew so much. What did your body grow from?
flow.kid: What helps you grow?

good: The food I eat.
Rice, dal, milk and fruit, and sleep.

flow.parent: Your body is built from the food you eat. A toy never grows, however much food you give it.

setup.art: A child's hand flat on paper, a grown-up drawing round it with a pencil, a date written beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw round your hand. Write the date.

setup.art: A child holding a tiny baby sock next to her own foot and laughing.
setup.caption: 2. Try on a baby sock. Does it fit?

activities.title: A Tomato Full of Young
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up cuts a tomato in half, and you look at the seeds inside. Each seed is a young tomato plant, waiting to grow.

materials.item: a knife and a chopping board, for the grown-up

schedule.what: Cut a tomato in half. Look at the seeds. Count the seeds on a spoon.

activities.record: Draw the cut tomato and the seeds.

flow.do: Cut the tomato across the middle, not from top to bottom. Show both halves.
flow.say: Look inside the tomato. What do you see?
flow.kid: Look inside. What are the little round things?

ask.q: What are the little things inside?
good: Seeds.
Baby tomato plants.

flow.do: Scoop out one spoonful of seeds onto the plate. Count them with your child.
flow.say: Let's count the seeds in one spoonful.
flow.kid: Count the seeds. Touch each one as you count.
flow.parent: A ripe tomato has many seeds, often more than 100. Counting a spoonful is enough.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: If we planted all of these, what would happen?
flow.kid: What would grow from these seeds?

check.q: What can grow from a tomato seed?
options: A tomato that is already ripe
check.why: A tomato seed is alive, resting inside the fruit. With soil and water, the seed grows into a young tomato plant. This is how plants have young.

setup.art: A grown-up's hands cutting a red tomato in half across the middle on a wooden chopping board.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts the tomato across the middle.

setup.art: A child counting small tomato seeds on a white plate with one finger.
setup.caption: 2. Look at the seeds. Count one spoonful.

activities.title: Window Watch: what is alive out there?
activities.context: In this activity you look out of a window or a balcony for five minutes, and count the living things you see.

schedule.what: Look out of a window for five minutes. Make a mark for every living thing you see.

activities.record: A mark for each living thing, and a drawing of your favourite one.

flow.do: 1. Sit by a window or on the balcony. 2. Each time your child spots a living thing, they make one mark on the paper.
flow.say: Let's look out of the window. Every time you see something alive, make a mark. Trees count too!
flow.kid: Look out of the window. See something alive? Make a mark.
flow.parent: Crows, pigeons, mynas, sparrows, trees, potted plants, grass, ants on the wall, dogs and people all count. In a city flat there is almost always a crow or a pigeon within five minutes.

flow.do: Count the marks together. Ask the question below.
flow.say: How many living things did you find? Which one surprised you?
flow.kid: Count your marks. How many?

ask.q: How did you know each one was alive?
good: The crow was flying and eating.
The tree has green leaves and grows.

setup.art: A child at a city flat window, looking out at a crow on a ledge and a tree across the road, with a paper of marks in hand.
setup.caption: 1. Look out for five minutes.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with nine pencil marks and a small drawing of a crow.
setup.caption: 2. A mark for each living thing.

projects.title: Mint Grows Roots
projects.context: In this two-week project you keep a mint sprig in a glass of water and watch for new roots. A picked sprig that grows roots is clearly still alive.

materials.item: two fresh mint (pudina) sprigs with long stalks
a clear glass or bottle of water

schedule.what: Pull the lowest leaves off two mint stalks. Stand them in a clear glass of water by a bright window.
Look for tiny white bumps on the stalk under the water. Change the water.
Look for white roots. Draw them. Change the water.
Look at the roots. Plant one sprig in a pot of soil if you have one.

projects.record: Draw the stalk under the water on day 1, day 4, day 8 and day 14.

flow.do: 1. Pull the leaves off the bottom part of each stalk. 2. Stand them in a clear glass of water. 3. Put the glass by a bright window, out of hot sun.
flow.say: Let's see if a picked mint sprig can grow. We'll check it every few days.
flow.kid: Take off the bottom leaves. Put the mint in water. Put it by the window.

flow.do: Look at the stalks under the water together. Change the water.
flow.say: Can you see any tiny white bumps on the stalk under the water?
flow.kid: Look under the water. Any white bumps?
flow.parent: Change the water every 3 or 4 days so it stays clean.

flow.do: Look for white roots. Draw them together. Change the water.
flow.say: Look! Are those roots? Where are they growing from?
flow.kid: Look for roots. Draw them.
flow.wait: Leave the glass for 4 more days.
flow.parent: Mint usually grows roots in about one or two weeks. In cold weather it can take longer. If one sprig goes brown and soft, take it out and keep watching the other.

flow.do: Look at the roots together and ask the question below. If you have a pot of soil, plant one sprig.
flow.say: The mint was picked from the plant. Now it has new roots. Is it alive?
flow.kid: The mint grew roots. Is it alive?
flow.wait: Leave the glass for 6 more days.

ask.q: How do you know the mint is alive?
good: Because it grew new roots.
Because it is growing, and growing is a sign of life.

setup.art: Two mint sprigs with their bottom leaves removed, standing in a clear glass of water on a windowsill.
setup.caption: 1. Stand two mint sprigs in a clear glass of water.

setup.art: The same glass two weeks later, with thin white roots growing from the stalks under the water.
setup.caption: 2. Look for white roots in one or two weeks.

challenges.title: Make a Toy That Seems Alive
challenges.context: This is a making challenge. You make a paper toy that seems alive. Then you check which signs of life your toy has.
challenges.problem: Can you make a toy that looks alive? It should move or seem to eat. Then we check: which signs of life does your toy really have?
constraints: Use only paper, card, string, tape and things from home.
materials: paper or card from an old box
general: A paper snake on a string that wiggles when you pull it.
A paper puppet with a mouth that opens and shuts, to 'eat' paper food.
A paper bird on a stick that flaps when you shake it.
creative: A paper fish that 'breathes' by puffing a little bag in and out when you squeeze it.
A paper plant that 'grows' when you pull a strip up out of a cup.
challenges.your_turn: Make your own toy that seems alive. Show it to someone at home. Then tell them which signs of life your toy has and which it does not.

flow.do: Read the challenge to your child. Show the materials.
flow.say: Let's make a toy that seems alive. It can move, or open its mouth to eat. What will you make?
flow.kid: Make a toy that seems alive. What will you make?

flow.do: Help your child make the toy. Cut where needed.
flow.say: How will you make it move? Which part will move?
flow.kid: Make your toy. How will it move?
flow.parent: Keep it simple: a folded paper snake on a string works well. Your child does the drawing and colouring.

flow.do: Play with the toy. Go through the signs of life one by one.
flow.say: Does your toy move? Does it eat? Does it grow? Does it breathe? Can it have babies?
flow.kid: Does your toy eat? Grow? Breathe? Have babies?

ask.q: Your toy moves. Is your toy alive?
good: No, it only moves when I pull it.
No, it does not eat, grow or have babies.

check.q: A paper snake wiggles when you pull the string. Why is the snake not alive?
options: Because the snake is made of paper and only moves when pulled
Because the snake is the wrong colour
Because the snake is too small
check.why: The paper snake only moves when someone pulls it. It never eats, grows, breathes or has young. A real snake does all of these by herself.

setup.art: A child folding a long strip of paper into a zigzag snake, with crayons and a piece of string on the table.
setup.caption: 1. Make a paper toy that seems alive.

setup.art: The child pulling the string so the paper snake wiggles across the floor, and a grandmother watching.
setup.caption: 2. Play with the toy. Check each sign of life.

items.p: Circle the living things in green. Circle the things that were never alive in red.
items.why: The crow, the tulsi plant and the ant eat, grow, breathe and have young. The stone, the spoon and salt never did any of these.
items.art: Six small drawings on a page: a crow, a stone, a tulsi plant, a steel spoon, an ant and a heap of salt.

items.p: Draw a line from each mother to her baby.
items.why: Every living thing has young, and the young grow up to be like the parent. A tadpole looks very different from a frog, but grows into one.
items.art: Four mothers on the left (hen, cow, frog, dog) and four babies on the right (puppy, tadpole, chick, calf), mixed up.

items.p: Which one is alive?
items.why: A cat eats, grows, moves, breathes and has kittens. A toy car and a ball never do these things by themselves.

items.p: A tree is alive.
items.why: True. A tree grows, makes food in their leaves, breathes through tiny holes in the leaves, and makes seeds. A strong answer gives one of these reasons.

items.p: Draw yourself breathing out on a cold steel plate. Draw what you saw on the plate.
items.a: A child and a plate with a cloudy patch on it.
items.why: Breath coming out of us is warm and wet. On a cool plate it makes a cloudy patch. A strong drawing shows the patch near the mouth.
items.art: A blank box with a small steel plate drawn in one corner.

items.p: Three of these were once alive. Which one was never alive?
items.why: The wooden spoon came from a tree. Cotton comes from a cotton plant. The dry leaf was on a tree. The steel tumbler was never part of a living thing.

items.p: The droopy mint stood up in water. The paper leaf did not. Why?
opts: The paper leaf was too big
items.why: Living mint fills up with water and goes firm. Paper only soaks up water and goes soggy. So the mint was still alive.

items.p: Draw one living thing you can see from your window.
items.a: Any living thing: a crow, a pigeon, a tree, a plant, a dog or a person.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a real living thing from the window, not a car or a building.
items.art: A blank window frame to draw inside.

items.p: The ceiling fan moves, so the fan is alive.
items.why: False. The fan moves only when it is switched on. It never eats, grows, breathes or has young. Moving alone does not mean alive.

items.p: Count the living things in this picture: two crows, one tree, a car, a dog and a house.
items.why: Two crows, one tree and one dog make 4 living things. The car and the house were never alive.
items.art: A street scene with two crows on a wire, one tree, a parked car, a dog and a house.

items.p: Put each thing on the right plate: once alive or never alive?
items.why: A coconut shell grew on a coconut tree. A newspaper is made from wood, from trees. The stone and the marble were never part of a living thing.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: how do you know you are alive? Give two reasons.
items.a: I eat food. I grow bigger. I breathe. I run and jump.
items.why: A strong answer gives two different signs of life, such as eating and growing, and says how the child does them.

items.p: Meena and her brother Ravi look at a potted plant on their balcony in Kochi.

views.says: The plant is not alive. The plant never moves.
The plant is alive. The plant grows new leaves.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing Ravi has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Meena, because the plant grows, makes food and breathes. Ravi is right that the plant does not walk around. But plants do move slowly, turning their leaves to the light.
items.why: Many young children think plants are not alive because plants stay in one place. Plants show the other signs of life, and they move too, only slowly.

items.p: Here are three plates. Label each one: alive, once alive or never alive.
labels: a plate with a potato and a mint sprig
a plate with a wooden spoon and a cotton cloth
a plate with a steel spoon and salt
a: wooden spoon and cotton: once alive
steel spoon and salt: never alive
items.why: The potato and the mint can still grow. The wooden spoon and the cotton came from plants. The steel and salt were never part of a living thing.
items.art: Three plates with things on them and an empty label under each plate.

items.p: Draw a baby animal and the grown-up animal they will become.
items.a: Any pair, such as a chick and a hen, or a caterpillar and a butterfly.
items.why: Young living things grow up to be like their parents. A strong drawing shows the same kind of animal, small and grown-up.
items.art: Two empty boxes with an arrow between them.

items.p: Is a potato alive?
opts: Yes, a potato can grow shoots
items.why: A potato left in a dark cupboard grows shoots after some weeks. A potato is alive, resting until the right time to grow. Being food does not stop a thing being alive.

items.p: Draw the mint in water before and after one hour.
items.a: A droopy mint sprig in the first picture, and the same sprig standing up in the second.
items.why: Living mint takes in water and stands up firm. A strong drawing shows the change clearly.
items.art: Two empty glasses side by side, labelled 'before' and 'after one hour'.

items.p: A dry tej patta from the kitchen is alive.
items.why: False. The tej patta was once alive, on a tree. Now it is dry. In our mint test, the tej patta did not stand up in water.

items.p: Fire grows bigger and needs air. Is fire alive?
opts: No, fire only burns the wood up
items.why: Fire grows and needs air, but fire never builds a body from food. Fire only burns things up and leaves ash. Scientists say fire is not alive. This one is tricky, so a child who thinks hard about it is doing well.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: a plant does not have a mouth. How does a plant eat?
items.a: A plant makes their own food in their green leaves, using sunlight, air and water.
items.why: A strong answer says plants make their own food, and names sunlight or the green leaves.

items.p: Put the mango story in order: from seed to tree.
items: A mango seed in the soil
A small seedling with two leaves
a: A mango seed in the soil
A small seedling with two leaves
items.why: The seed grows into a seedling, and the seedling grows into a tree. Growing is a sign of life.
items.art: Three small pictures, mixed up: a mango tree, a seed in soil, a seedling.

items.p: Lakshmi and her grandfather in Madurai look at a wooden chair.

views.says: The chair was never alive. A chair does not eat or grow.
The chair was once alive. The wood came from a tree.

items.ask: Who is right? Why? What does Grandfather have right?
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Lakshmi: the wood came from a living tree, so the chair was once alive. Grandfather is right that the chair does not eat or grow now.
items.why: Once alive means the thing was part of a living thing. The chair is not alive now, but the wood was part of a tree.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: The crow, the tree and the cat are alive. A cloud moves and grows bigger, but a cloud does not eat, breathe or have young. So the cloud is the odd one out.

items.p: Draw round your hand. Then draw what you think your hand will look like when you are grown up.
items.a: A hand outline, and a bigger hand drawn round it.
items.why: Children grow because they are alive. A strong drawing shows a bigger grown-up hand.

items.p: Match each sign of life to what you saw.
pairs: a cloudy patch on the steel plate
a baby sock that no longer fits
a snail scraping a cabbage leaf
items.why: Each thing we did showed one sign of life. A strong answer can say which activity showed each one.

items.p: An empty snail shell is lying behind a pot. What is it?
items.why: The shell was once part of a living snail, so it is once alive. No snail lives in it now.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: why did we leave one droopy mint sprig on a dry plate?
items.a: To see what happens without water. It stayed droopy, so the water made the other mint stand up.
items.why: A strong answer sees that the dry plate sprig shows what water did. Without it, we could not be sure the water made the difference.

items.p: Only animals have young. Plants do not.
items.why: False. Plants have young too. Seeds grow into new plants, and a mint sprig can even grow roots and become a new plant.

items.p: Label each part of the snail: shell, eyes, breathing hole.
labels: the round hard part on the back
the dots on top of the long horns
the small hole near the shell
a: dots on the long horns: eyes
small hole near the shell: breathing hole
items.why: A land snail carries a shell, has eyes at the tips of the long horns, and breathes through a hole on the side. A strong answer remembers the snail from the story.
items.art: A drawing of a land snail with three empty label lines pointing at the shell, the tips of the long horns and a small hole near the shell.

items.p: Priya counted 12 seeds in one spoonful of tomato. She took 2 spoonfuls. About how many seeds did she have?
items.why: 12 and 12 make 24. Every one of those seeds could grow into a new tomato plant.

quiz.why: A stone was never part of a living thing. The coconut shell and the dry leaf came from trees, so they were once alive.
The crow eats, flies, breathes and lays eggs. The wooden spoon was once alive. The steel plate was never alive.
Cotton comes from the cotton plant. The shirt is not alive now, but it was part of a living plant.

quiz.p: Which of these is a sign of life?
quiz.why: Living things grow. A steel spoon is shiny and hard, and was never alive.

quiz.p: You breathed on a cool steel plate. What did you see?
quiz.why: Your breath is warm and wet. On a cool plate it makes a cloudy patch. Breathing is a sign of life.

opts: No, the plant stays in the pot
Yes, the plant grows and makes seeds
quiz.why: Plants grow, make food, breathe and make seeds. Staying in one place does not mean a thing is not alive.

quiz.p: What is the young of a cow called?
quiz.why: A calf is the young of a cow. A kid is a young goat. A chick is a young bird.

quiz.p: A tadpole grows up to be…
quiz.why: A tadpole hatches from a frog's egg, grows legs and loses the tail, and becomes a frog.

quiz.p: In the mint test, what happened to the droopy mint in water?
opts: The mint stood up firm again
The mint went soggy like paper
quiz.why: The mint stood up, because the picked mint was still alive and filled up with water. The paper only went soggy.

quiz.p: A toy robot walks and talks. Is the robot alive?
opts: No, the robot does not eat, grow or have young
quiz.why: Moving and making sounds are not enough. A robot does not grow, eat food or have baby robots, so a robot was never alive.

videos.title: A land snail eating a leaf, close up
videos.why: See a snail's horns, eyes and breathing hole up close, like the snail in the story.
videos.check: Find a real, calm close-up of a land snail feeding, under 5 minutes, with no scary music.

videos.title: Mint cuttings growing roots in water, time-lapse
videos.why: Shows in two minutes what the mint project shows in two weeks.
videos.check: Find a real time-lapse of mint or another herb rooting in water.

videos.title: A wilted plant recovering after watering, time-lapse
videos.why: Shows a droopy plant standing up again after water, like the mint test.
videos.check: Find a real time-lapse, not animation, of a wilted plant recovering.

applications: Doctors check if a person is breathing, to see if they need help.
Farmers and gardeners keep picked greens in water or in a cool, damp cloth so they stay fresh longer.
Gardeners grow new mint, money plants and roses from cut stalks.
Scientists looking for life on other planets look for signs of life, such as breathing out gases.

spotted.text: A vegetable seller in the market sprinkling water on coriander and palak to keep them fresh.
spotted.art: A woman at a vegetable cart sprinkling water from her hand onto bunches of green coriander.

spotted.text: A money plant growing in a bottle of water on a kitchen window, with long white roots.
spotted.art: A money plant in a glass bottle on a window, with white roots in the water.

spotted.text: A crow on the balcony rail, eating a bit of chapati, then flying away.
spotted.art: A crow on a balcony rail holding a piece of food in her beak.

spotted.text: Snails on wet walls and pots during the monsoon in Mumbai, Kochi or Goa.
spotted.art: A snail climbing a wet wall beside a flower pot.

spotted.text: A potato or an onion in the kitchen basket growing green shoots.
spotted.art: An onion in a basket with a green shoot growing from the top.

open_questions.q: Exactly when does a picked leaf stop being alive?
open_questions.why_open: The tiny parts inside a leaf die a few at a time, over days. Scientists do not agree on one moment when the whole leaf is no longer alive.

open_questions.q: How did the very first living thing begin?
open_questions.why_open: Every living thing today comes from another living thing. But long ago there must have been a first one. Scientists have ideas, but nobody knows for sure.

open_questions.q: Is there life on other planets?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists are looking, with telescopes and robots on Mars. So far they have not found any living thing beyond Earth.

ask_kids: Is anything on your plate alive? Was it alive once?
On the way out, can you spot three living things and one thing that was never alive?
What did you do today that shows you are alive?
Is the rice we eat alive, once alive or never alive?
If you could ask a crow one question about being alive, what would you ask?

jokes.j: Why did the snail carry their house everywhere?
jokes.a: Because the snail never wanted to be late for home!

jokes.j: What did the steel spoon say to the mint leaf?
jokes.a: You're so fresh! I'm just stainless.

jokes.j: Why didn't the stone eat breakfast?
jokes.a: Because the stone was never hungry, not once in a million years!

jokes.j: What do you call a baby cow who likes to dance?

jokes.a: Because the tomato saw the salad dressing!

jokes.j: What did the tadpole say when he grew legs?
jokes.a: Now I can hop to it!

jokes.j: Why does the ceiling fan never get a birthday cake?
jokes.a: Because the fan never grows a year older!

jokes.j: How does a mint plant say hello?
What does a crow say at the window every morning?
jokes.a: Caw-me in, I'm alive and hungry!

maths.problem: Ishita sorted her kitchen things. On the alive plate she put 2 things. On the once alive plate she put 4 things. On the never alive plate she put 3 things. Which plate had the most?
maths.answer: The once alive plate had the most, with 4 things.
maths.explain: 2, 4 and 3. 4 is bigger than 3, and 3 is bigger than 2. So the once alive plate had the most. Many kitchen things come from plants and animals.
maths.context: This is about the three plates activity, where you sorted kitchen things into alive, once alive and never alive.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the plates shows that many kitchen things were once part of a living thing.

maths.problem: From the window, Divya saw 3 crows, 2 pigeons and 1 tree. How many living things did she see?
maths.explain: 3 crows and 2 pigeons make 5. Add 1 tree and you get 6. The tree counts, because trees are alive.
maths.context: This is about the window watch, where you made a mark for every living thing you saw.
maths.why_maths: Making a mark for each living thing and counting them shows how much life is around us, even in a city.

maths.problem: The mint sprig grew 3 roots by day 8 and 7 roots by day 14. How many more roots grew between day 8 and day 14?
maths.explain: Start at 3 and count on to 7: 4, 5, 6, 7. That is 4 more roots. The mint kept growing, so the mint was alive.
maths.context: This is about the mint project, where a picked mint sprig in water grew new roots over two weeks.
maths.why_maths: Counting on from one day to the next shows the mint was still growing, and growing is a sign of life.

warmup.q: Name one thing that is alive.
warmup.a: A crow, a tree, an ant, a plant or you.

warmup.q: Is a stone alive, once alive or never alive?
Is a wooden spoon alive, once alive or never alive?
warmup.a: Once alive. It came from a tree.
Eating, growing, moving, breathing or having young.

warmup.q: What is the young of a hen called?

warmup.a: Yes. Plants grow, make food, breathe and make seeds.

founder: ideas/by_topic/living-and-non-living-signs-of-life.md: alive, once alive and never alive; signs of life. The SCI cards there (Lynn Margulis, Venkatraman Ramakrishnan) are for higher levels and were not used here.
science: Wilting and recovery: leaves droop when their living cells lose water and stand up again when the cells refill (turgor). Dead, dried leaves cannot do this. Any plant biology textbook.
Mint (Mentha) stem cuttings root readily in water, usually within one to two weeks.
Maria Sibylla Merian, Der Raupen wunderbare Verwandlung (1679) and Metamorphosis insectorum Surinamensium (1705).
Robert Brown, 'A brief account of microscopical observations' (1828), on the movement of tiny particles in water, seen in 1827.
Land snails (Stylommatophora): eyes on the upper tentacles, breathing through a pneumostome, feeding with a radula.
Cambridge Primary Science Stage 1, Unit 1 'Being alive'.

roots.context: We have learned how to tell what is alive, once alive and never alive. Now we ask what the droopy mint tells us about being alive.

deep_truth.truth: Our mint was picked before we bought it, and the sprigs had gone droopy. In a cup of water, they stood up firm again. The dry tej patta and the paper leaf stayed as they were. So a picked sprig stays alive for days, and living does not stop the moment we pick.
deep_truth.habit: We think a thing is either alive or dead, and that picking a leaf ends their life at once. The mint shows that going from alive to once alive is slow, and takes days.
deep_truth.evidence: In the mint test, droopy picked mint stood up firm in water within about an hour, but the dry tej patta did not change. In the mint project, a picked sprig grew new roots in a glass of water.

three.who_am_i: You are alive. You eat, grow, move and breathe every day, even while you sleep.
three.what_is_life: Life is something a body keeps doing: taking in water and food, growing and making more. The picked mint kept doing it for days.
three.what_is_this_world: Many things around us were once alive: the wooden spoon, the cotton shirt, the paper in your book. Living things become part of the world around them.

roots.thread: The mint, the snail, the crow and you are all alive, each in their own way. All life on Earth comes from other life, going back a very long time. The wooden spoon and the paper were part of that life once. Everything is conscious, and every living thing feels and acts in their own way. The mint feels the water, and takes it in.

teachings.teaching: When people are born, they are soft and bendy. When they die, they are stiff and hard. Plants are soft and full of sap while they live. When they die, they are dry and brittle.
teachings.link: We felt this in the mint test. The living mint was soft, and stood up full of water. The dry tej patta was stiff and brittle, and water could not bring it back.

teachings.teaching: Sharing your food and caring for all living beings is the best of all that the wise have taught.
teachings.link: Every living thing needs food and water. The Tirukkural, from Tamil Nadu, asks us to share them with all living beings, not only people.

science.text: Picked leaves stay alive for some days. Their tiny living parts can still take in water, which makes a droopy leaf firm again. Dry, dead leaves cannot do this.
Scientists do not agree on one exact moment when a picked leaf stops being alive.

other_view.view: A picked sprig is a living part of a plant, not a whole living plant. They say the sprig is alive only in the sense that its tiny parts are still living, until it grows roots of its own.

practice.title: Soft leaf, dry leaf
practice.say: Close your eyes. Hold out both hands. I will put a fresh leaf in one hand and a dry leaf in the other. Feel each one gently. Which one is alive? Now put your hand on your tummy. Breathe in slowly, and out slowly. Feel your own body, soft and warm and alive.
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Hold out both hands. Feel each leaf. Which one is alive? Now breathe in slowly. Breathe out slowly. Feel your tummy move.

ask: When we pick a leaf, when does the leaf stop being alive?
Is a little bit of the tree still in the wooden spoon?
What would you need to stay alive if you were the mint in the glass?
roots.art: A child with eyes closed, holding a fresh green mint sprig in one open hand and a dry brown tej patta in the other.

how_we_found_out.story: About 350 years ago, many people in Europe believed that some small animals were not born from parents. They thought caterpillars, flies and worms grew out of mud, rotting leaves or old meat. Maria Sibylla Merian was born in Frankfurt, in Germany, in 1647. When she was about 13, she began to keep caterpillars at home. She fed each one the leaves they liked and watched them every day. She saw butterflies lay tiny eggs on leaves. She saw caterpillars hatch from the eggs, eat and grow, and then turn into butterflies. She painted every step, with the plant each caterpillar ate. In 1679 she published a book of her paintings. Later, when she was 52, she sailed to Suriname in South America with her daughter Dorothea, and painted the insects and plants there. Her pictures showed clearly that a caterpillar comes from a butterfly's egg. Every living thing comes from another living thing.
how_we_found_out.who: Maria Sibylla Merian, a German painter and scientist, with her daughter Dorothea
how_we_found_out.when: 1660 (when she began) to 1705 (her book on the insects of Suriname)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That small animals such as caterpillars, flies and worms grow by themselves out of mud, rotting leaves or old meat, without parents.
